## Abstract

Objectives: Community health screening programs frequently report inconsistent follow-up rates and barriers to sustained lifestyle changes. This study evaluated the HealthStart program, a layperson-led intergenerational health coaching program that aims to improve health screening follow-up, chronic disease understanding and ownership, digital health application adoption and sustained lifestyle changes.

Methods: HealthStart is a self-determination theory-based intervention that aims to increase the autonomy and competence of participants via volunteer engagement, health coaching, and post-health screening follow-up. Lay volunteers (LVs) were taught principles of motivational interviewing, health coaching and social determinants of health via a training model anchored on principles of intergenerational and service learning. LVs act as health advocates through the participants’ journeys under the guidance of healthcare volunteers. Convergent parallel mixed-methods analysis was employed. A total of 192 participants’ quantitative data were collected through pre- and post-program surveys. Qualitative data were obtained from 36 semi-structured interviews analyzed through thematic analysis.

Results: The follow-up rate among primary care providers increased significantly from 42.7% to 84.5% (?2=43, p<0.001). A total of 66.2% (92/139) of the participants achieved their health goals, and 81.3% (113/139) reported satisfaction with the program. There was a statistically significant correlation (Z=2.44, p=0.015) between participant health goal attainment and the number of follow-up visits and between post-cycle participant eHealth literacy scale (eHEALS) scores and the number of followup visits (F(2,130)=6.06, p=0.003). The qualitative findings highlighted LVs’ crucial role in facilitating health conversations, promoting lifestyle changes, and building meaningful connections in catalyzing lifestyle changes in the participants. While the training adequately prepared LVs for these tasks, some encountered challenges with participants resistant to change or with complex needs.

Conclusion: HealthStart demonstrated the feasibility and impact of using laypersons in the community to increase follow-up

## Background

## Introduction

Many  countries  are  facing  an  aging  population[1],  with  a  rising  prevalence  of  chronic

diseases[2]. Community health screenings are key preventive health programs aimed at

screening, detecting, and managing these conditions. However, these screening programs

report inconsistent follow-up rates[3,4], and many patients experience barriers to sustained

lifestyle changes, including a lack of knowledge and community support[5]. In the United

States, many cancer screening programs involve fewer than 75% of patients receiving

some form of follow-up care[6]. In 2016, SingHealth, Singapore’s largest public healthcare

cluster,  reported  that  one  in  four  individuals  screened  via  community-based  health

screenings had not returned for a doctor’s follow-up after a year[7]. Loss to follow-up has

significant physical and socioeconomic implications, including untreated chronic conditions,

physical  complications,  reduced  healthcare  system  efficiency,  and  increased  financial

costs[8].

While lay volunteers (LVs) have been effectively utilized in specific screening programs for

screening follow-up, such as the blood cholesterol screening, counseling, and referral

(SCORE) system under the Pawtucket Heart Health Program (PHHP) in the 1990s[9] and

the Baltimore eye screening program in the early 2000s[10], their role in broader screening

programs addressing major cardiovascular risk factors and health coaching has not been

thoroughly investigated.

With appropriate training, LVs can be empowered to guide health screening participants in

navigating the health system, increasing follow-up rates, setting specific health-related

https://preprints.jmir.org/preprint/75699 [unpublished, non-peer-reviewed preprint]

lifestyle goals, and adhering to them. Previous qualitative studies have shown benefits of

this  approach,  including  improved  person-focused  coordinated  care[11],  more  seamless

referrals to  appropriate  services[12],  and  the  promotion  of  healthy  practices[13].  Experts

recommend measuring indicators that predict the success of lay counselors[14] and exploring

their effectiveness in more complex tasks, such as diagnosis and counseling [15]. When

designed  and  implemented  appropriately,  community-based  health  coaching  has  the

potential to be a significant nonclinical intervention for individual and population health[16],

simultaneously improving the health literacy of health coaches undergoing training and the

general public and facilitating the adoption of healthy practices across generations[17].

Conceptual Framework

HealthStart is a self-determination theory (SDT)-based intervention built to support the

Healthier SG (HSG) initiative, the local government’s policy to promote healthier aging by

reshaping  the  population’s health-seeking  behaviors and  lifestyle  through  collaborative

community-based  care[18]. It  aims  to  increase  the  engagement  and  follow-up  rates  of

participants  attending  a  chronic  disease  community  health  screening  by  developing,

training, and empowering LVs to be health advocates that accompany participants in their

postscreening journey over a three-month period.

SDT proposes that personally relevant goals are more internally motivated and are thus

more likely to be obtained than goals set due to some external pressure [19]. It specifies three

basic psychological needs (i.e., autonomy, competence, and relatedness) that provide the

basis for motivation and development and are the contextual conditions that facilitate

internal motivation and help people integrate their behavior into their everyday lives and

sense of self. Autonomy refers to the sense that one’s actions are the result of their own

https://preprints.jmir.org/preprint/75699 [unpublished, non-peer-reviewed preprint]


<!-- Page 11 -->


JMIR Preprints Yow et al

volition, competence is the belief in one’s ability to affect change and achieve desired

outcomes, and relatedness is the extent to which one feels a connection with others. Self-

integration  of  behaviors  occurs  when  externally  motivated  behaviors  (i.e.,  behaviors

regulated by an external force) become integrated into one’s ‘sense of self’; that is, they

contribute to one’s overall evaluation of the self.

HealthStart aims to increase the autonomy and competence of the participants through the

SDT framework via volunteer engagement, health coaching, and posthealth screening

follow-up, relating that to the participants’ lifestyle to increase knowledge, confidence, and

digital  health  literacy  and  set  and  achieve  lifestyle  goals.  The  SMART  (Specific,

Measurable, Achievable, Realistic, and Timely) framework is used to assist participants in

setting lifestyle-related goals and achieving sustained lifestyle change[20]. LVs are taught

health knowledge and health coaching skills, which they applied through their interaction

with participants under the guidance of healthcare volunteers (HCVs) who underwent a

preprogram facilitation workshop. The program’s theory of change is reflected in Figure 1.

Volunteer  training  in  HealthStart  is  delivered  via  a  blended  learning  approach[21] and

anchored  on  principles  of  intergenerational  and  service  learning,  combining  learning

objectives  with  community  service  to  create  a  meaningful  learning  experience  while

meeting the community needs of older adults[22]. Youths with no prior healthcare experience

are recruited as LVs. On an individual level, lifelong health habits are best cultivated at a

young  age,  and  there  is potential  to  improve  health  literacy among  youths[23].  At  the

community level, having imparted LVs with a service learning experience in HealthStart,

there is potential for intergenerational transfer of health knowledge when LVs bring the

knowledge  and  experience  gained  from  the  program  back  to  their  families  and

communities[24]. The concept of service learning emphasizes volunteers’ learning through

critical reflection by having them participate in community service experiences in real-world

settings; this aspect is grounded in Kolb’s experiential learning theory, which states that

https://preprints.jmir.org/preprint/75699 [unpublished, non-peer-reviewed preprint]


<!-- Page 13 -->


JMIR Preprints Yow et al

effective  learning  is  based  on  concrete  experience,  reflective  observation,  abstract

conceptualization and active experimentation[25]. The HealthStart program is intentionally

designed to achieve reciprocity by valuing both volunteer learning experiences and the

benefits for the recipient[26].

Contact theory was used to guide intergenerational program development and study[27].

There are four main tenets that, when present in the contact setting, increase the likelihood

that people will experience positive contact: the support of governing bodies, equal group

status,  intergroup  cooperation,  and  common  goals.  In  the  design  of  the  HealthStart

program, we built upon lessons learned in a previous intergenerational program that was

demonstrated  to  increase  health  literacy  and  reduce  ageist  attitudes[28].  The  program

emphasized the concept of equal group status, where all the volunteers attended the

training day together and were collectively held accountable for the participants whom they

were  assigned.  Intergroup  cooperation  and  common  goals  were  also  built  into  the

interactions between the LVs and the participants, where they devised a plan together and

fulfilled the goals set out at the start of the program. Throughout the journey, HCVs,

comprising doctors and nurses, act as clinicians who teach healthcare knowledge and skills

to LVs and as mentors who provide supervision to LVs as they engage with the participants.

The primary outcome of the program was residents’ enrollment with a family physician.

Each resident had to additionally complete a local health promotion board (HPB) booklet [29]

detailing their newly diagnosed condition, learn a digital health application, and set a

healthy lifestyle goal and achieve it. The secondary outcomes include increases in health

knowledge, health ownership and digital health literacy among residents, as well as the

acceptability of the program among stakeholders.

## Methods

Program Implementation

For the participants, the program consists of a personal review of their health screening

results,  health  goal  setting  with  their  assigned  LVs,  follow-up  with  their  PCPs,  and

completion of their health goals over a three-month duration. Throughout the process,

HCVs oversee the operations and provide avenues for content clarification and professional

support as necessary. Each HealthStart group consists of one HCV and four LVs. Each LV

is assigned two participants. LVs are expected to follow up with participants over a period of

three months through either physical or virtual visits.

To complete the HealthStart program, participants will need to fulfill the following criteria:

1. Learn about their chronic disease(s) with the aid of the Health Promotion Board

(HPB) booklets[29]

2. Learn at least one digital health application such as HealthHub[30,31]

3. Enrollment with a PCP

4. Set a lifestyle goal and achieve it

The participants will first meet their LVs at a community event where health screening

reports are distributed and explained by a community nurse. The LVs will conduct their first

session of health coaching with the participants and build rapport via questions that cover

sociodemographic factors and lifestyle aspects (exercise, smoking, alcohol intake, dietary

habits), utilizing tools such as a time wheel and a healthy plate (Appendix 1) to aid them.

The time wheel provides the participants and  LVs with a clearer picture of their time

allocation within a 24-hour period to identify pockets of time for purposeful healthy lifestyle

https://preprints.jmir.org/preprint/75699 [unpublished, non-peer-reviewed preprint]


<!-- Page 15 -->


JMIR Preprints Yow et al

changes  (e.g.,  brisk  walking,  meal  planning).  The  Healthy  Plate  acts  as  a  guide  for

participants and LVs to review the current dietary content of their meals and in conjunction

with the time wheel to find time for either healthy cooking or to travel for healthier food

options.

LVs subsequently teach participants about their newly diagnosed chronic disease via HPB

educational materials, guide them in the use of digital health applications [30,31], assist in

setting up an appointment to a PCP through the use of the digital health application

HealthHub and support the participants in setting a lifestyle goal. LVs follow up with their

participants one-to-one longitudinally over a period of 3 months through in-person or virtual

visits (i.e., video calls) every fortnight, where they check the participants’ progress, motivate

them to achieve their goals, and ensure the fulfillment of the program’s four goals.

LVs are required to fill out a follow-up visit form after each visit and a final visit form at the

last visit to track the participant’s progress through HealthStart and have monthly meetings

with LVs to reflect on their intergenerational and service-learning experience. This provides

a chance for  LVs to practice the mentoring skills learned and is an extension of Kolb’s

experiential learning within small groups[25].

Volunteer Training

The HealthStart training adopts a blended learning approach[21]. Volunteers are divided into

teams from the outset to facilitate team building. This early introduction fostered bonding

within  the  team  throughout  the  training  process.  All  volunteers  are  provided  with  an

overview  of  the  program  and  the  operational  aspects  of  HealthStart  for  baseline

understanding. LVs are trained to be health coaches by watching prerecorded lectures on

the following topics: Singapore’s healthcare system, chronic diseases and principles of

https://preprints.jmir.org/preprint/75699 [unpublished, non-peer-reviewed preprint]


<!-- Page 16 -->


JMIR Preprints Yow et al

management, social determinants of health, and vital sign monitoring. Educational materials

by  the  Health  Promotion  Board  Singapore  on  the  following  conditions  (hypertension,

hyperlipidemia, and diabetes mellitus) and a volunteer protocol guidebook (Appendix 2) for

operational workflow reference are sent to the volunteers.

LVs are required to take a pretraining quiz to ensure adequate knowledge acquisition prior

to in-person training. This is followed by interactive lectures covering topics related to

SMART  goal  setting  and  the  principles  of  motivational  interviewing.  HCVs  undergo

workshops on community healthcare, social determinants of health (SDOH), mentoring and

facilitation training. The facilitation workshop aims to equip HCVs with knowledge and basic

skills for mentoring LVs and to foster stronger intergenerational relationships through the

HealthStart journey. The in-person training session takes place over a day.

The training day ends with HCVs and LVs gathering back in their groups to play the various

scenarios they may encounter and provide an opportunity for HCVs to interact with the LVs

and put into practice mentoring and facilitation skills. An organizing committee member role

plays a role as a participant in these scenarios and acts to monitor the dynamics and

provide support and feedback as needed. There are four scenarios simulating the various

scenarios in the entire journey that the LVs may encounter (Appendix 3). Each scenario is

followed by a debrief session led by the group’s HCV and a large group reflection for all

volunteers. This structure provides opportunities for reflective observation and encourages

volunteers  to  practice  abstract  conceptualization,  applying  what  they  have  learned  to

subsequent  scenarios,  in  line  with  Kolb’s  experiential  learning  cycle[25].  HCVs  use  a

standardized evaluation checklist to assess the competency of  LVs (Appendix 4).  LVs

deemed  unsuitable  for  the  health  coaching  role  are  offered  additional  training  or

opportunities to volunteer in other capacities.

Study Design

This study used a convergent parallel mixed-methods design to evaluate the effectiveness

of the HealthStart program. This outcome evaluation aimed to determine 1) the health

impact on older adults and 2) the acceptability of the program among older adults, HCVs

and LVs.

Participants

Older adults aged 40 years and above who participated in the health screening, LVs aged

21--35  years  and  HCVs  who  participated  in  the  program were  eligible  for the  study.

Individuals  with  medical  comorbidities  that  affected  their  ability  to  communicate  (e.g.,

severe dementia) were excluded from the study. Individuals who could not speak English,

Mandarin, Malay, or Tamil were also excluded.

Quantitative Data Collection and Analysis

The quantitative data collection was conducted between September 2022 and June 2023.

Data from older adults were collected at the beginning of the health screening and at the

end (third month) of each cycle through a digital survey administered by a trained volunteer.

The data were collected via FormSG, a secure electronic government-encrypted web-

based form with the following designed fields.

1. Sociodemographic  variables,  including  age,  sex,  race,  marital  status,  highest

education level, and residential type

2. Primary outcome: Follow-up with a primary care doctor, measured as ‘Yes’ or ‘No’

3. Secondary outcomes

a. Knowledge  Questionnaire:  a  12-item  true/false  questionnaire  on  chronic

https://preprints.jmir.org/preprint/75699 [unpublished, non-peer-reviewed preprint]


<!-- Page 18 -->


JMIR Preprints Yow et al

conditions that is an abbreviated version of the 15-minute chronic disease

questionnaire[32] adapted to the local context using information from the Health

Promotion Board (HPB) brochures

b. Patient  Activation  Measure  (PAM-13):  a  13-item  questionnaire  measuring

individuals'  ability  to  self-manage  chronic  disease  through  self-reported

knowledge, skills, and confidence[33].

c. eHealth  Literacy  Scale  (eHEALS):  an  8-item  questionnaire  assessing

respondents' perceived skills in using information technology for health[34].

d. SMART (Specific, Measurable, Attainable, Relevant, Time-based)[20] health

goal attainment: self-rated achievement of lifestyle goals, measured as a ‘Yes’

or ‘No’

e. Program satisfaction: "To what extent are you satisfied with the program?"

with  4-level  Likert  scale  response  options  (not  at  all  satisfied,  slightly

unsatisfied, slightly satisfied, very satisfied).

Descriptive statistics were computed for the study population. The program implementation

fidelity was tracked via the number of follow-up visits and the number of final assessments

conducted. McNemar’s test was used to examine differences in the proportion of primary

care  follow-up  before  and  after  the  program.  Pre- and  postintervention  differences in

secondary outcomes were compared via paired t tests. One-way ANOVA and linear trend

tests were employed in the subgroup analysis to evaluate the relationships between the

secondary outcomes and the number of follow-up visits the residents received. A binomial

logistic regression was performed with primary care follow-up as the outcome variable and

demographics  and  baseline  questionnaire  scores  as  the  predictor  variables.  All  the

statistical analyses were performed via Stata Version 15 (StataCorp. 2017. Stata Statistical

Software: Release 15. College Station, TX: StataCorp LLC.) Statistical significance was set

Qualitative Data Collection and Analysis

Qualitative data were collected through one-to-one, semistructured interviews with older

adults, LVs, and HCVs who participated in the program. Purposive sampling was used to

recruit older adults on the basis of the following criteria to ensure the representability of

each group: age, sex, race, education level, number of follow-up visits within the program

and postprogram primary care follow-up status. Convenience sampling was used for LVs

and HCVs. The interview guides were formulated on the basis of the reconstructed theory

of change to elicit perceptions of the program, the health advocacy process with older

adults, and the volunteer training program (Annex 1).

The interviews were conducted between November 2023 and January 2024 face-to-face or

via Zoom Web Conferencing (Zoom Video Communications, Inc., San Jose, California) by

four project team members trained and supervised by the qualitative lead coinvestigator.

Each interviewer was trained in qualitative data collection techniques. All interviews were

audio-recorded and transcribed via an automated transcription software service and later

checked  by  a  project  member,  ensuring  verbatim  accuracy  and  redacting  identifiable

information. Four team members coded the transcripts via a deductive-abductive approach,

focusing on perceptions toward the program, the health advocacy process, and volunteer

training while allowing new themes to emerge. Thematic analysis, following the framework

of  Braun  and  Clarke[35],  was  used  by  four  coders  to  analyze  the  transcripts.  After

independently  coding  the  transcripts,  a  secondary  coder  reviewed  them  to  address

discrepancies and finalize the coding. QSR NVivo 14 software was employed for data

management and analysis. Data triangulation was used to identify areas where qualitative

## Results

Quantitative

HealthStart  reached  out  to  192  older  adults  via  30  healthcare  workers  and  115  lay

volunteers over two health screening cycles conducted in 2022 and 2023, respectively.

## Discussion

The postprogram primary care provider follow-up rate was 84.5%, which was higher than

previously reported rates in health screening programs[6,7]. The binomial logistic regression

revealed that older adults and minority races were significantly correlated with a higher

primary care provider follow-up rate. A 2019 study in Taiwan revealed that elderly people

were more likely to participate in preventive health screening than younger people were [36],

similar to the findings of this study. Minority race groups have been shown to have lower

screening follow-up rates than majority race groups in previous studies[37]. HealthStart was

offered freely to all residents regardless of race; deliberately linked LVs with older adults

who spoke the same mother tongue; and provided an educational booklet in the older

adult’s  mother  tongue  language  to  facilitate  accessibility,  communication,  and

understanding, which likely helped reduce racial inequity[38].

The health goal attainment rate was 66.2%, with individuals being more likely to achieve

them if they had more LV follow-ups. The majority of goals centered on improving one’s diet

or physical activity. A total of 54.5% of a group of 33 participants achieved their set health

goal in a previous community outreach health coaching program conducted by certified

health coaches in Missouri[39]. This study revealed equivalent rates of health goal attainment

in older adults receiving abnormal health screening results, with their postscreening journey

facilitated by lay volunteers. The qualitative findings highlighted a key takeaway of the

program  being  understanding,  planning  for,  and  achieving  healthy  lifestyle  changes,

facilitated by health coaching. The initial shock of receiving abnormal health screening

results from older adults may have formed an additional impetus for the high health-related

goal attainment rate[40]. Building on residents’ autonomy and competence through the SDT

framework[19] helped improve awareness of healthy practices and achieve health-related

https://preprints.jmir.org/preprint/75699 [unpublished, non-peer-reviewed preprint]


<!-- Page 31 -->


JMIR Preprints Yow et al

lifestyle changes in the HealthStart program.

The participants in this study were noted to have high baseline knowledge (8.81/12, SD =

1.58) and high PAM-13 scores (68.8/100, SD = 1.56), reflecting readiness to adopt new

behaviors but potentially having difficulty sustaining change[41], and relatively low eHEL

scores (24.5/40, SD = 0.92). There was no statistically significant change in knowledge of

chronic diseases, the PAM-13, or eHEALs between pre- and postintervention. Qualitative

interviews  revealed  that  most  older  adults  did  not  recall  specific  facts  about  chronic

diseases or adopt specific digital skills but learned more about the importance of health and

achieving health-related lifestyle changes through the program.

Despite  a  thorough  training  program,  LVs  faced  challenges  when  interacting  with

participants who were less keen or were not ready or motivated to make lifestyle changes

or those with complex psychosocial issues. In adapting to a new and often unfamiliar role,

dealing with different levels of individual receptivity and health system-level challenges are

among some of the key challenges faced by health coaches in the literature that were

similarly  described  in  HealthStart[42].  Qualitative  interviews  revealed  the  importance  of

having  professional  support  and  guidance  from  HCVs.  To  address  varying  levels  of

individual receptivity and health system-level challenges, incorporating the transtheoretical

model of change and a social prescription model with community resources for financial or

psychosocial  support  into  the  training  program  is  planned  in  future  iterations  of  the

program[43]. The reflection process on such challenges in an effort to learn and adapt to their

role formed a critical aspect of the LVs’ learning journey as part of  Kolb’s experiential

learning theory[25].

High  satisfaction  scores  were  reported  by  older  adults  of  the  program  (81.3%),  and

qualitative reports demonstrated acceptability and appreciation for the program from both

https://preprints.jmir.org/preprint/75699 [unpublished, non-peer-reviewed preprint]


<!-- Page 32 -->


JMIR Preprints Yow et al

volunteers and older adults. LVs felt it was a rich experience and expressed interest in

volunteering in similar programs again. Older adults valued the new health insights gained

and reported improvements in their health and lifestyles. A qualitative study in Canada that

integrated community volunteers as extensions of the primary care team to support older

adults yielded similar findings. These community volunteers deepened the primary care

team's understanding of their patients and facilitated the delivery of person-centered care,

demonstrating the possibility of integrating community volunteers into the primary care

setting[11]. A separate study conducted in Canada revealed that community volunteers can

play a role in increasing older adults’ understanding of community resources and system

navigation[12]. LVs are potentially untapped resources capable of effectively engaging in and

promoting healthier living among older adults.

This study suggests that laypersons may be capable of improving primary care follow-up

rates  and  promoting  healthier  living  among  older  adults  when  equipped  with  chronic

disease knowledge and health coaching skills. The high acceptability and positive feedback

among all stakeholders suggest that laypersons can be valuable assets in population-level

preventive health initiatives, especially when supported by professional guidance. Given the

effectiveness, acceptability, potential reach and adoption of HealthStart, the evaluation

demonstrates the potential to scale community programs involving laypersons in population

health initiatives[44]. Program sustainability is further strengthened by collaborative work with

local grassroots organizations and alignment with the national strategic context of healthier

aging[45].

Strengths and Limitations

There are several limitations to this study. First, the observed improvements could not be

https://preprints.jmir.org/preprint/75699 [unpublished, non-peer-reviewed preprint]


<!-- Page 33 -->


JMIR Preprints Yow et al

attributed to the program due to the absence of a control group, and the majority of the

studies’ quantitative  outcomes  were  based  on  self-reported  scales.  Nevertheless,  the

qualitative data collected substantiate the study’s findings. Future studies could employ

more rigorous designs, such as quasiexperimental trials, to establish causality. Additionally,

participant attrition resulted in missing data, which introduces the potential for nonresponse

bias. The strengths of the study include the mixed methods evaluation, which allows for the

triangulation of data and the inclusion of significant numbers of traditionally underserved

populations, such as ethnic minorities and individuals of low socioeconomic status.

## Conclusion

This study demonstrated the feasibility of utilizing laypersons to improve follow-up rates and

promote healthier lifestyles among older adults participating in community health screening.

The  high  acceptability  of  this  model  among  stakeholders  highlights  the  potential  of

harnessing the community, an untapped valuable resource, in population health initiatives.
